name: Times Literary Supplement cryptic crossword No 1,129

solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique, linked answer split by the grid); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing; the grid proves the blog's enumeration wrong at 4 down, recounted from the answer here

clue.text: Lamb opens these Kipling poems about start of Lammas

indicators.note: the start of a word is just its opening letter
to be about something is to surround it, so one piece wraps round another

blocks.note: The Seven Seas is Kipling's 1896 collection of poems
Lammas is the August 1st harvest festival; its first letter

explanation.surface: An essayist named Lamb opens a book of Kipling's verse around Lammas, the early August harvest festival.
explanation.walkthrough: Lamb is not Charles Lamb the essayist but the Lamb of the Book of Revelation, who breaks open the seals one by one.
explanation.definitionFit: In Revelation the Lamb alone is worthy to break the seven seals of the scroll held by God.

clue.text: Closes 17A, say and shouts out very loudlly

indicators.note: something put out of order is disarranged, so these letters are rearranged

blocks.note: taken as written
ff, fortissimo, is the musical marking for very loud

explanation.surface: Someone shuts things noisily and yells at the top of their voice.
explanation.walkthrough: 17A is GAS TAP, so the definition is what you do to a gas tap. 'Loudlly' is misprinted in the source; ff is the score marking fortissimo.
explanation.definitionFit: To shut off a tap or supply is to close it so nothing flows; a gas tap is a typical example.

clue.text: Too too much in convoluted dud movie – not one to be seen

indicators.note: something convoluted is twisted and tangled, so the letters are rearranged
saying a thing is not there means it is taken away

blocks.note: taken as written
O resembles the figure for one; it is the letter removed
n stands for an indefinitely large number, more than enough

explanation.surface: A critic finds a muddled flop of a film overdone and best left unwatched.
explanation.walkthrough: Remove O from DUD MOVIE, add N for an indefinite excess, and rearrange. The answer is a Latin gerundive borrowed into English.
explanation.definitionFit: Videndum is Latin for a thing that ought to be seen, used in English for something worth viewing.

clue.text: Strive like little Malcolm

blocks.note: first meaning: to make a great effort against difficulty
second meaning: from David Halliwell's play title about Little Malcolm and his fight against the eunuchs

explanation.walkthrough: 'Little Malcolm and His Struggle Against the Eunuchs' is a 1965 play by David Halliwell, so the word is what Malcolm has.
explanation.definitionFit: The verb means to exert oneself hard, and the noun is the fight in the title of Halliwell's play.

clue.text: Hope like Burgess?

blocks.note: first sense: the forename of the author of 'The Prisoner of Zenda'
second sense: the forename of the author of 'A Clockwork Orange'

explanation.walkthrough: Hope is not optimism but a surname: Anthony Hope and Anthony Burgess were both English novelists, so each surname leads to the same forename.
explanation.definitionFit: Both writers bore this given name, so the forename is what Hope shares with Burgess.

clue.text: Jameson’s may have ruined “The Lovely Ship”

blocks.note: first sense: the novelist Jameson's forename with a possessive
second sense: violent weather that wrecks vessels

explanation.surface: Something belonging to Jameson might have spoiled her novel 'The Lovely Ship'.
explanation.walkthrough: Storm Jameson wrote 'The Lovely Ship' (1927), so 'Jameson's' is her forename plus 's, and gales at sea wreck ships.
explanation.definitionFit: Margaret Storm Jameson went by her middle name, and violent gales at sea are what founder vessels.

clue.text: Are they suitable to encompass new appreciation of music by soprano?

definitions.text: Are they suitable to encompass new appreciation of music by soprano?

indicators.note: to encompass is to surround, so one piece goes round others

blocks.note: fit means suitable
N is the abbreviation for new
an ear for music is an appreciation of it
S is the abbreviation for soprano

explanation.surface: A question about whether something is apt to include a fresh love of music sung by a soprano.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue doubles as a description: music, appreciated by ear and sung by sopranos, is one of the arts the answer names.
explanation.definitionFit: The fine arts are the creative disciplines, music among them, valued for beauty rather than use.

clue.text: Sort of method actor

blocks.note: a brand is a sort or kind
o' is the clipped form of 'of', as in o'clock

explanation.surface: A hedging description of a performer who is more or less a Method actor.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sort of' reads as a hedge, but it is two pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: Marlon Brando was the most famous exponent of Method acting, trained by Stella Adler at the Actors Studio.

clue.text: One of nine rings for mortals endlessly involved with just one

indicators.note: without its ends, only the inside of the word is kept
involved means tangled up, so the letters are mixed together

blocks.note: the word with its first and last letters lopped
I is the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: A Tolkien echo: the nine rings given to mortal men, tangled up with the One Ring.
explanation.walkthrough: The nine rings evoke Tolkien, but the nine are from Dorothy L. Sayers' 'The Nine Tailors', strokes of a church bell tolled for a death.
explanation.definitionFit: In change-ringing a tailor (teller) is one of the nine strokes rung to mark a man's death.

clue.text: Riders to end all races

annotation.answer: THE FOUR HORSEMEN OF THE APOCALYPSE

blocks.note: surface reading: jockeys in some final, decisive horse race
setter's reading: mounted figures who bring the end of all peoples of the world

explanation.walkthrough: Races means peoples, not contests. The four riders of Revelation bring conquest, war, famine and death; Blasco Ibáñez also used the title for a novel.
explanation.definitionFit: The four mounted figures of Revelation herald the end times, destroying the nations of mankind.

clue.text: “Yes, sir – fourth spell of penal. You’d think an – like him would have more sense by now.” (John Galsworthy)

definitions.text: “Yes, sir – fourth spell of penal. You’d think an – like him would have more sense by now.” (John Galsworthy)

blocks.note: surface reading: a quotation with a gap to be filled

blocks.clueFragment: would have more sense by now
blocks.note: setter's reading: a habitual criminal serving his fourth stretch of penal servitude

explanation.walkthrough: The quotation is from Galsworthy's play 'Escape'; the gap is filled by British slang for a convict who keeps returning to prison.
explanation.definitionFit: A man on his fourth spell of penal servitude is a hardened repeat offender, a veteran prisoner.

clue.text: A tale of the seaboard featuring Italian bosun

blocks.note: first meaning: the subtitle of Joseph Conrad's 1904 novel
second meaning: its title character, an Italian boatswain in the port of Sulaco

explanation.walkthrough: Conrad's novel is subtitled 'A Tale of the Seaboard', and it is named after its hero, a Genoese former bosun.
explanation.definitionFit: The novel takes its name from its protagonist, whose nickname is Italian for 'our man'.

clue.text: Greek ready to be found in “Remnants”

indicators.note: something found in a word is sitting inside it, ready to be lifted out

blocks.note: the middle letters of the word

explanation.surface: Something Greek is waiting among the remnants.
explanation.walkthrough: Ready here is a noun: 'the ready' is British slang for cash, not the adjective meaning prepared.
explanation.definitionFit: The mna or mina was an ancient Greek unit of weight and money, so it is Greek cash.

clue.text: Put down Hergesheimer’s romance with 4

blocks.note: first meaning: to place something down
second meaning: the first word of Joseph Hergesheimer's 1914 romance, completed by 4's answer

explanation.walkthrough: 4 is ANTHONY, and Hergesheimer's novel is 'The Lay Anthony', so the missing word is the other half of the title.
explanation.definitionFit: The verb means to set something down, and it also completes the title of Hergesheimer's first-person romance.

clue.text: Preventing which Joseph achieved brief renown in Egypt at first

definitions.note: the answer replaces 'which': Joseph achieved preventing this

indicators.note: kept brief means cut short, so the last letter is lost
what comes at first is the opening letter only

blocks.note: fame, with its tail docked
taken as written
the opening letter of the country

explanation.surface: Joseph won fleeting fame in Egypt at the start of his career.
explanation.walkthrough: In Genesis Joseph read Pharaoh's dream and stored grain through seven plentiful years, so Egypt survived the seven lean ones.
explanation.definitionFit: Joseph's grain stores averted starvation, a severe food shortage, during seven bad harvests in Egypt.

clue.text: Literary anecdotes doing the rounds; no change there then?

indicators.note: nothing changes when the word is turned about, so it reads alike both ways

blocks.note: turned round, the word is still the same

explanation.surface: Bookish gossip keeps circulating, and the story never changes.
explanation.walkthrough: There is no fodder here: the definition alone gives the word, and the tail tells you it reads the same backwards.
explanation.definitionFit: Ana is a collection of sayings, table talk or anecdotes about a writer, from the suffix in Johnsoniana.

clue.text: Like the last part of “The Rainbow” – that’s about one that’s poor

definitions.text: Like the last part of “The Rainbow”

indicators.note: to be about something is to surround it, so one piece wraps the rest

blocks.note: i.e. is short for id est, Latin for 'that is'
an is the indefinite article, meaning one
thin means meagre or poor

explanation.surface: Someone discusses the closing section of D. H. Lawrence's novel and a poor character in it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The Rainbow' is Lawrence's novel, but here it is a real rainbow, whose last band is violet.
explanation.definitionFit: The adjective means violet-coloured, from the Greek for violet flower, the final colour of a rainbow's spectrum.

clue.text: With which to start laughing in Wodehouse?

definitions.text: With which to start laughing in Wodehouse?

blocks.clueFragment: With which to start laughing in Wodehouse?
blocks.note: surface reading: what sets a reader of Wodehouse's comedy giggling
setter's reading: 'Laughing Gas' is a Wodehouse novel, and you turn on the gas with a fitting on the supply pipe

explanation.walkthrough: Wodehouse wrote a 1936 novel called 'Laughing Gas'; the device that starts any gas flowing is the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A valve on a supply pipe is turned to release the gas, so it starts the laughing gas.

clue.text: Stern retailer – he’ll have cheered him up

blocks.note: grim means stern
Aldi is a discount supermarket chain

explanation.surface: A severe shopkeeper who would have lifted a customer's spirits.
explanation.walkthrough: Joseph Grimaldi was the great Regency clown; 'him' is the reader of the clue, or any glum Londoner of his day, whom a clown would cheer.
explanation.definitionFit: Joseph Grimaldi, the most famous English clown, made audiences laugh at Sadler's Wells and Drury Lane.

clue.text: Shine at start of play, performing? I might

indicators.note: the start of a word is just its opening letter
letters that perform are put through their paces into a new arrangement

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written
the first letter of the word

explanation.surface: An actor hoping to excel at the opening of a play asks whether they themselves might be performing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'I might' is the definition: the answer, speaking, says it might be performing. The question mark flags the stretch.
explanation.definitionFit: An actor is the one who might perform; the word comes from Thespis, the first Greek actor.

clue.text: Was she worthy of Pearl Curran?

definitions.text: Was she worthy of Pearl Curran?

blocks.clueFragment: Was she worthy of Pearl Curran?
blocks.note: surface reading: was some woman deserving of Mrs Curran?
setter's reading: 'worthy' points to the surname Worth of the spirit the St Louis medium claimed to channel

explanation.walkthrough: Pearl Curran, an American medium, said her books were dictated by a 17th-century spirit called Patience Worth; 'worthy' hides that surname.
explanation.definitionFit: The spirit author's given name, the woman whose surname was Worth, is the one Curran channelled.

clue.text: Where minstrel boy went, unprepared to return

indicators.note: to return is to go back the way you came, so the letters run backwards

blocks.note: raw means unprepared, as of untrained recruits or uncooked food

explanation.surface: The young singer of the song went off unready, never to come home.
explanation.walkthrough: Thomas Moore's song begins 'The Minstrel Boy to the war is gone', so the definition is a destination.
explanation.definitionFit: In Moore's Irish ballad the young harper leaves for battle and dies fighting, so armed conflict is where he went.

clue.text: Was about to disapprove of medium used by “The Waggoner”

definitions.note: a description of the trees by their use, not a synonym

indicators.note: to be about something is to surround it, so one piece is split round the rest

blocks.note: taken as written
to boo is to jeer in disapproval
M is the abbreviation for medium, as on clothes labels

explanation.surface: Someone was on the verge of frowning on the style of a work called 'The Waggoner'.
explanation.walkthrough: The waboom is a South African protea, the 'wagon tree', whose tough wood was used for wagon wheels, so a waggoner would use it.
explanation.definitionFit: Waboom is Afrikaans for wagon tree; its hard timber served Cape wagon-builders and drivers for wheels and brakes.

clue.text: “Mage” is an alternative to Jonson’s “Alchemist”, like marchesite or tutie

definitions.text: to Jonson’s “Alchemist”, like marchesite or tutie

indicators.note: an alternative is another version, so the letters take another form

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A wizard is offered as a substitute for Ben Jonson's play about an alchemist and his mineral jargon.
explanation.walkthrough: In 'The Alchemist' Subtle reels off 'your marcasite, your tutie, your magnesia'; the word sits in that list of substances.
explanation.definitionFit: Magnesia was an alchemical mineral, named alongside marcasite and tutty in the jargon Jonson's tricksters spout.

clue.text: Jane Smiley novel in German, sounding bovine

blocks.note: 'Moo' is Jane Smiley's 1995 campus novel
taken as written
G is the abbreviation for German

explanation.surface: A Jane Smiley novel in German translation sounds like a cow.
explanation.walkthrough: Smiley's 'Moo' is set at an agricultural college, which suits the bovine definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Cows low, and making that deep call is what a cow does when it sounds off.

clue.text: “Now you have no – on your head” (Twelfth Night)

definitions.text: “Now you have no – on your head” (Twelfth Night)

blocks.note: surface reading: a quotation with a gap to be filled
setter's reading: Antonio, a ship's master, is told his mariner's headgear is missing as he is arrested

explanation.walkthrough: In Act 3 an officer arresting Antonio, a ship's captain, says he is known 'though now you have no' sailor's hat on.
explanation.definitionFit: A seaman's cap identified Antonio as a mariner; the officer recognises him even without it.

clue.text: Acting most like Jerome, for fear that I’d come first

indicators.note: what comes first is placed at the front of the sequence

blocks.note: the contraction without its apostrophe
lest means for fear that

explanation.surface: Someone behaves like Jerome out of fear of being beaten to first place.
explanation.walkthrough: Jerome K. Jerome wrote 'Idle Thoughts of an Idle Fellow' and edited 'The Idler', so to be most like him is to be laziest.
explanation.definitionFit: Jerome cultivated the persona of a lazy fellow, so behaving most like him means being the laziest.

clue.text: See 9
Fictional land, reflecting one in Kurosawa film

indicators.note: a reflection shows things mirrored, the wrong way round

blocks.note: a means one
taken as written
'Ran' is Kurosawa's 1985 version of King Lear

explanation.surface: An invented country is mirrored by one appearing in a Japanese film.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In' looks like a container instruction, but it is a piece of the string that is turned round.
explanation.definitionFit: C. S. Lewis's Chronicles are set in an imaginary kingdom entered through a wardrobe.

clue.text: Plague involved in “Celestine Prophecy” initially

indicators.note: involved means tangled up, so the letters are mixed together
initially means at the beginning, so only the first letter counts

blocks.note: taken as written
the first letter of the word

explanation.surface: A plague features in the early part of James Redfield's bestseller 'The Celestine Prophecy'.
explanation.walkthrough: With 9 and 24, this completes the theme: Pestilence is one of the four riders, alongside war, famine and death.
explanation.definitionFit: A pestilence is a deadly epidemic disease, the sense in which a plague sweeps a population.
